passage:
[1] The first thing my teacher told me about the potter's wheel was that it would not care how much I wanted the clay to behave. Mrs. Adeyemi ran the ceramics room at the community center on Tuesday nights, she had a habit of saying difficult things while looking at something else. She was scraping dried slip off a bat when she said it. I laughed, because I assumed she was joking. She was not.

[2] Centering is the step that comes before anything you would recognize as pottery. You slap a lump of clay onto the spinning, rotating wheel head, brace your elbows against your thighs, and pressing inward and downward until the lump stops wobbling and turns as a perfect, humming cone. Done well, it takes about a minute. Similarly, done the way I did it that first month, it takes forty minutes and ends with a lopsided mass sliding off the wheel and onto my shoes.

[3] [A] The problem, Mrs. Adeyemi finally explained, was that I was fighting the clay instead of holding it. [B] Every time the lump lurched to one side I chased it, my hands jerking after the wobble, and the wobble simply moved. [C] What the clay needed was a pair of hands that stayed still and let the wheel bring the clay to them. [D] "You are not the one turning," she said. "Stop acting like it."

[4] The night it finally worked, I was not concentrating especially hard. Having braced my arms and pressed, my mind drifted to the dishes waiting at home, when I noticed that the sound of the wheel had changed. The scraping rhythm had smoothed into a steady hum, and under my palms the clay had gone quiet. I opened my eyes, which I had not realized were closed. The cone was centered.

[5] I have cranked out a ton of bowls since then, and I have given most of them away. I still think that the most useful thing I learned in that room had nothing to do with bowls. Some problems cannot be chased. You hold steady, and you let them come to you.

explanation: The subject of the verb is the singular "thing," not the nearer plural-sounding noun in the prepositional phrase, so the singular "was" agrees with it. A plural verb breaks that agreement, a comma between subject and verb is never allowed, and "being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

passage_title: The Lantern That Runs on Waves
passage:
[1] For most of her career, Ilse Marrow worked on problems nobody else considered interesting. As the harbor engineer for the town of Corrigan Point, she was responsible for the pilings, the breakwater, and the dozen channel markers that guided fishing boats past the sandbar at the mouth of the bay. Corrigan Point was a pleasant town in most seasons. Each marker ran on a battery that had to be replaced by boat every few weeks; and in winter, when the swells were highest and the battery runs most dangerous, the lights failed most often.

[2] Marrow's idea was to let the waves that threatened the markers power them instead. Inside each buoy she installed a weighted pendulum that moved with every rise and fall of the water. The pendulum turned a small generator, and it charged a battery pack no larger than a paperback book. The rougher the sea, the brighter the light. On a calm night the battery held enough charge to last for a week.

[3] The first prototype sank. The second floated but flooded. The third, which Marrow bolted together in her garage over the winter of her fifty-first year, staying lit through a March gale that knocked out three of the town's conventional markers. The harbor board, who had approved her project mostly to stop her from bringing it up at meetings, voted the next month to replace every marker in the channel.

[4] Marrow never patented the design. When a manufacturer in another state offered to license it, she sent back a sketch of the pendulum housing and a note that read, "Build it better." Today, at the present time, variations on her buoy mark channels along hundreds of miles of coastline. Most of the people who rely on them have never heard her name, which is, by all accounts, exactly how she preferred it.

choices: The breakwater had never quite done what it was built to do.
The pilings were rotting faster than the town could replace them.
explanation: The sentences that follow explain why the channel markers kept failing. A sentence that names the markers as the trouble sets up that explanation directly. A remark about the town's pleasantness, or a sentence that names the breakwater or the pilings as the problem, points the reader toward something the rest of the paragraph never discusses.

passage:
[1] Seen from an airplane, a river crossing a flat valley rarely runs straight. It swings from side to side in wide, looping curves called meanders, and although the pattern looks fixed, it is not. Over decades and centuries a meander moves across its valley, sometimes by several feet a year, and the river slowly rewrites the map.

[2] The movement begins with a small difference in speed. Water on the outside of a bend has farther to travel than water on the inside, so it moves faster. Fast water carries more energy, and energy is what it takes to deal with sand and clay on a bank. The outside of the bend therefore erodes; while the slower water on the inside drops the sediment it can no longer carry. A bar of sand and gravel built up on the inside of the curve at the same time that the outside curve is being cut away.

[3] [A] The result is that the bend migrates. [B] Erosion on the outside pushes the curve outward and downstream, and deposition on the inside follows behind it, filling in the space the river has abandoned. [C] Because each bend moves this way, the whole loop grows wider and more exaggerated, until the river is nearly doubling back on itself. [D]

[4] Eventually the loop becomes so tight that the narrow neck of land between it's two arms is only a few yards across. During a flood, when the river is high and fast, the water may simply cut through the neck and take the shorter path. The old loop, now ditched, is left as a crescent of still water called an oxbow lake. With time it silts up, grows over with reeds, and becomes a curved scar in the fields, visible mainly to the airplane passenger who happens to look down.

[5] Farmers and towns have long fought this restlessness, lining banks with stone and concrete to hold a river in place. The fights are costly, and they are rarely permanent. Sooner or later, a river in a flat valley will do what rivers there have always done, and move.

passage:
[1] Last spring, the hardware store on Harlow Street closed after sixty years, and the lot behind it has sat empty ever since. The city has floated several ideas for the space, including a parking annex and a small commercial building. I would like to propose a third option; a neighborhood tool library, open to any resident with a library card.

[2] A tool library works the way a book library does. Instead of novels, the shelves hold drills, ladders, tile saws, and pressure washers, and members borrow them for a week at a time. The model is not new. Dozens of cities have run tool libraries for years, and the ones I have visited share a familiar rhythm on Saturday mornings: a line of neighbors at the counter, trading advice as much as equipment.

[3] The practical case is strong. Most households use a power drill for less than fifteen minutes a year, yet each of them own a drill, a set of bits, and a charger gathering dust in a closet. A shared collection lets a block of forty houses own one good, high-quality drill instead of forty mediocre ones. Renters, whom are unlikely to buy a ladder they cannot store, gain access to tools they would otherwise go without. And every borrowed item is one fewer purchase that ends up in a landfill after a single use.

[4] The social case is stronger. A parking annex asks nothing of anyone and gives nothing back. A tool library asks neighbors to show up, sign a card, and return what they borrowed in working order, and it gives them a reason to engage in interpersonal dialogue with one another. In an era when many of us cannot name the people three doors down, that is not a small thing.

[5] The lot is already zoned for community use, and the hardware stores old shelving is still inside the building. The city council takes public comment on the site next month. I hope Harlow Street will show up with a proposal of its own.

[1] Curling looks, to a first-time spectator, like a game invented to fill a long winter. Two teams of four slide forty-pound granite stones down a sheet of ice toward a target painted beneath the surface, and the team who's stones finish closest to the center scores. The whole thing proceeds at a walking pace. Then a stone is released, two players with brooms begin sweeping the ice in front of it with a lot of effort, and the pace no longer looks slow.

[2] The sweeping is not for show. A curling sheet is not smooth; before each game it is sprayed with droplets of water that freeze into a pebbled texture. A stone rides on the tops of these pebbles. Sweeping warms the ice just enough to melt a thin film on the pebbles, which reduces friction, but a swept stone travels farther and curls less than an unswept one. Deciding when to sweep, and how hard, are the difference between a stone that stops on the button and one that slides through the house and out of play.

[3] The game has kept traditions that most sports shed long ago. Players call their own fouls. A stone touched by a broom is removed from play by the team that touched it, without waiting to be told. Matches begin and end with handshakes, and a team that falls hopelessly behind is expected to concede and give up rather than run out the clock. [A] After the game, by long custom, the winners buy the losers a drink, and the two teams sit down together. [B] Curlers call this "broomstacking," from the days when players propped their brooms against the wall of the clubhouse before joining the table. [C] Newcomers sometimes find these customs quaint. [D]

[4] They are also the reason the game survives in small towns where no other winter sport does. A curling club needs a sheet of ice, a set of stones that will last a century, and to have people willing to spend an evening being polite to their opponents. Where those three things exist, the game tends to stay.
